info.bio:
Billy Guy, miembro de los Coasters y uno de los mejores barítonos del doo wop y del rhythm and blues de finales de los años 50, nació en Texas el 20 de junio de 1936.

The Coasters comenzó su trayectoria  con la publicación del single "Down in Mexico" que en 1956 alcanzó el Top Ten de las listas de éxitos de R&B de Estados Unidos. Este tema fue incluido en la banda sonora de la película Death Proof de Quentin Taratino que es, por cierto, un gran fan de los Coasters.

scenes.name: Antes del diluvio
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La «edad oscura» del rock'n'roll: los rebeldes son sustituidos por ídolos adolescentes educados y el Brill Building devuelve el poder a los compositores profesionales. Pero en esos años se incuban la revolución futura: la guitarra fuzz de Link Wray, los bailes de moda (el twist), el rock instrumental de guitarras (Duane Eddy, Ventures, Shadows), el calipso y el primer ska, el doo-wop más inventivo (Coasters, Drifters, Five Royales), el nacimiento del soul (Sam Cooke, Ray Charles, Motown, Stax), el estudio como instrumento de Joe Meek y el surf de los Beach Boys y del «muro de sonido» de Phil Spector.

podcast.title: Classic Lineup Formed (1957)
podcast.body: The Coasters' classic lineup, featuring Cornel Gunter and Doug Jones, who replaced Leon Hughes and Bobby Nun, finally fell into place. This formation occurred after a year during which the group had not had a hit, as their writing and production team, Jerry Lieber and Mike Stoller, were focused on more lucrative work with artists like Elvis Presley. "The classic lineup of the coasters had finally fallen into place, but it had been a year since they had had a hit."

podcast.title: Leiber and Stoller's Post-Elvis Work (Post-1958)
podcast.body: After their definitive professional break with Elvis and subsequent loss of jobs at RCA, The Coasters were among the prominent R&B artists that Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller concentrated on writing for. "The Coasters."

podcast.title: Audience Segmentation
podcast.body: The Coasters had two distinct audiences: an R&B audience, largely composed of older black people, and a white teenage audience. Different songs appealed more to each group, highlighting a distinction in how black performers' music was received when singing for a black audience versus a white one. "I think it makes a difference, as well, that the coasters had two different audiences. They had an R&B audience, who were mostly older black people, and they had a white teenage audience."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Commercial Decline and Production Changes
podcast.body: Following the attempt to transition to the adult market and the album "One by One" failing to garner success, The Coasters' commercial fortunes entered a terminal decline. During this period, Lieber and Stoller ceased to be the exclusive producers for the group; several recordings were instead credited to Sill and Hazelwood, though these efforts also failed to achieve significant commercial success. "By this time, the group's commercial fortunes seemed to be in terminal decline."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Desperate Flailing for New Styles
podcast.body: Following a decline in chart success and a shift away from teenage-oriented material, The Coasters entered a period described as "desperate flailing about to try new styles." This included releasing an old standard, "Bessermé Moucho," a single written by a group member, Billy Guy's "Wake me Shake Me," and attempting yet another style with "Shopping for Clothes." "There seems to have been a sort of desperate flailing about to try new styles."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Legacy as Comedy Group
podcast.body: The Coasters were often dismissed as merely a "comedy group," yet their unique ability to create music that was both funny and musically worthwhile is considered one of the hardest achievements in the industry. Their comedy music has remained enjoyable for over 60 years, a feat that no other rock and roll act has replicated. "They were often dismissed as just a comedy group but as anyone who has ever tried it knows making music that is both funny and musically worthwhile is one of the hardest things you can do."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Lieber & Stoller's Direction
podcast.body: From the beginning of Lieber and Stoller's career, Jerry Lieber consistently directed the lead vocalist on how to sing his lines. This approach was applied to all artists they produced, including Elvis, Ruth Brown, and The Coasters, requiring them to follow Lieber's phrasing as closely as possible, a method that had previously annoyed Big Mama Thornton with "Hound Dog." "When Lieber and Stoller produced an artist, whether it was Elvis or Ruth Brown or the coasters or whoever, they would get them to follow Lieber's phrasing as closely as possible."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Manager Lester Sill Mentors Phil Spector
podcast.body: Lester Sill, who was Lieber and Stoller's mentor in their early years and The Coasters' manager, introduced a young musician named Phil Spector to the songwriting and production duo. Spector, an admirer of Lieber and Stoller who had a hit with "To Know Him Is To Love Him" with his group The Teddy Bears, was seeking an apprenticeship. As a favor to Sill, Lieber and Stoller signed Spector to a publishing contract, gave him jobs as a session guitarist, and allowed him to sleep in their office or Lieber's spare room. "Lester Siller said that the kid in question was a huge admirer of Leibor and Stuller, and wanted to learn from them."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Post-Hit Lineup Instability and Rival Groups
podcast.body: After their last significant hit, "Little Egypt," Cornel Gunter left to sing with Dinah Washington, later forming his own "Coasters" group which, despite not being allowed to record under that name, toured extensively with the support of Dick Clark. Billy Guy also pursued a solo career, often sending a replacement on the road while still recording with the main group, and his solo records sometimes were reissued under The Coasters' name without other members' involvement. Over decades, nearly everyone involved with The Coasters started rival versions of the group, with Carl Gardner retaining legal rights to the name, but others performing as "Cornel Gunter's Coasters" or "Leon Hughes and his Coasters." "Over the next few decades, pretty much everyone who'd been involved with The Coasters started up their own rival version of the group."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Racist Stereotypes Criticism
podcast.body: The Coasters' records faced criticism, notably from Johnny Otis and Charlie Gillett, for allegedly perpetuating racist stereotypes. Otis, who had personal issues with Lieber and Stoller regarding "Hound Dog" credits, specifically singled out "Charlie Brown." The group's performances, particularly Dub Jones' vocal parts, were clearly rooted in traditions of African American comedy that reappropriated stereotypes, but the controversy arose because the black performers were directed by two white writers, Lieber and Stoller, on how to perform these songs. "Johnny Otis in particular would make this criticism of the group's records, and it's one that must be taken seriously."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Shift from Teenage Focus
podcast.body: After "Poison Ivy," The Coasters' last Top 10 hit, Jerry Lieber and Mike Stoller seemed to grow bored of writing songs aimed at a teenage audience. Subsequently, most of the group's songs reverted to an older style, similar to that used with The Robins, focusing on social commentary and more adult topics. "Poison Ivy would be the group's last top ten hit, and it seemed to signal Lee Brunstoller getting bored with writing songs aimed at an audience of teenagers."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Transition to Adult Market Attempt
podcast.body: Around the release of "Shopping for Clothes," The Coasters became aware that their time as a pop chart act with a teenage fan base was ending. Carl Gardner, who had long wished to be a big band singer, pushed the group to attempt a transition into the adult white market, targeting audiences who bought records by artists like Tony Bennett or Andy Williams, a move encouraged by his friend Johnny Otis. "Around the time that shopping for clothes came out, the group became conscious that their time as a pop chart act with a teenage fan base was probably close to its end, and they decided to do something that Carl Gardner had wanted to do for a while, and tried to transition into the adult white market."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Violent Deaths of Associates
podcast.body: Several individuals associated with The Coasters met violent ends. King Curtis was stabbed to death in the street in 1971 at age 37 during an altercation outside his apartment building when he asked two people engaged in a drug deal to move so he could carry in an air conditioning unit. In 1980, one of Cornel Gunter's Coasters was murdered by Gunter's manager after threatening to expose the manager's criminal activities. Finally, Cornel Gunter himself was shot dead in 1990, with his killer never found. "Sadly, several people associated with the coasters ended up dying violently."
